18.about: Rachmaninoff’s most beloved and frequently performed concerto, marking his triumphant return to composition after a severe depression and creative paralysis following the disastrous 1897 premiere of his First Symphony. Its sweeping opening chords, soaring melodies and hard-won emotional journey from darkness to triumph have made it one of the most popular concertos ever written.
18.ctx: Composed in 1900–01 after months of therapy with the physician Nikolai Dahl, whose hypnosis-based treatment Rachmaninoff credited with restoring his ability to compose; the concerto is dedicated to Dahl in gratitude. Its success re-established Rachmaninoff’s career and remains, over a century later, one of the most recorded and performed works in the entire concerto repertoire.
parts: Famous for its tolling opening piano chords leading into a passionate main theme.
A serene, deeply lyrical slow movement.
A vigorous finale that transforms its themes into a triumphant close.
facts: Dedicated to Dr. Nikolai Dahl, whose treatment helped Rachmaninoff overcome a severe creative block.
Marked his return to composing after the failed premiere of his First Symphony.
One of the most popular and frequently performed piano concertos ever written.

27.about: A large-scale, richly melodic symphony, in particular its third movement, an extended Adagio built on one of Rachmaninoff’s most celebrated melodies, which has been adapted into popular songs and used widely in film. Composed as an act of redemption after the traumatic failure of his First Symphony a decade earlier.
27.ctx: Composed in 1906–07 while Rachmaninoff was living in Dresden, partly to escape the demands of his busy Moscow performing career and concentrate on composition, the symphony was a triumphant success at its premiere, helping to heal the deep insecurity left by his earlier symphonic failure.
parts: A brooding introduction leading to a sweeping main movement.
The symphony’s famous, richly melodic slow movement.
facts: Its slow movement contains one of Rachmaninoff’s most famous melodies.
Composed in Dresden, partly to escape his demanding Moscow concert schedule.
A triumphant success that helped heal the wounds of his earlier symphonic failure.

29.about: A somber orchestral tone poem inspired by Arnold Böcklin’s famous painting of the same name, depicting a shrouded figure being rowed toward a mysterious island of cypress trees and tombs. Built in an unusual, irregular 5/8 metre suggesting the slow, uneven strokes of oars, the piece grows increasingly turbulent before subsiding into a hushed, resigned close.
29.ctx: Composed in 1908–09 in Dresden, inspired specifically by a black-and-white photographic reproduction of Böcklin’s painting rather than the original, which Rachmaninoff reportedly found less striking in colour; quotes the Dies irae chant recurrent throughout his output.
facts: Inspired by Arnold Böcklin’s painting of the same name.
Rachmaninoff based it on a black-and-white photograph of the painting rather than the coloured original.
Written in an unusual 5/8 metre suggesting the rhythm of oars.

30.about: Nicknamed ’Rach 3’ by pianists, one of the most technically formidable concertos in the repertoire, composed for Rachmaninoff’s first American tour and dedicated to the pianist Josef Hofmann, who reportedly never performed it in public, considering it not suited to his own hands. Its immense difficulty and emotional scope made it, decades later, the subject of the 1996 film Shine.
30.ctx: Composed in 1909 at Ivanovka in preparation for Rachmaninoff’s debut tour of the United States, where he premiered it himself in New York that November under the young conductor Walter Damrosch, and again weeks later under Gustav Mahler, of whose rehearsal discipline Rachmaninoff spoke admiringly.
parts: A famous, deceptively simple opening theme leading to enormous technical and emotional demands.
facts: Popularly nicknamed ’Rach 3’ for its extraordinary technical demands.
Its dedicatee, Josef Hofmann, reportedly never performed it publicly.
The subject of the 1996 film Shine, about pianist David Helfgott.

36.about: A large-scale, densely virtuosic sonata that Rachmaninoff substantially revised nearly two decades after its composition, cutting and simplifying its most sprawling passages; both versions remain in the repertoire, with pianists divided over which better represents the composer’s intentions.
36.ctx: Composed in 1913 while Rachmaninoff was staying in Rome, in rooms once used by Tchaikovsky’s brother, and extensively revised in 1931 into a shorter, leaner version, reflecting Rachmaninoff’s own later view that the original had been overwritten.
parts: A turbulent, densely written opening movement.
facts: Rachmaninoff extensively revised the sonata in 1931, nearly two decades after its premiere.
Both the 1913 and 1931 versions remain in active use by performers today.
Composed in rooms in Rome once used by Tchaikovsky’s brother.

42.about: A set of twenty variations on a theme by Corelli (in fact borrowed, unknowingly by Corelli himself, from an older Portuguese folk tune known as ’La Folia’), alternating brilliant virtuosity with passages of stark, austere beauty; among the last solo piano works Rachmaninoff completed.
42.ctx: Composed in 1931 in Switzerland, where Rachmaninoff had settled after leaving Russia, the piece reflects the leaner, more concentrated style of his later works, a contrast to the lush Romantic sweep of his earlier Russian-period music.
facts: Based on the ’La Folia’ theme long misattributed to Corelli.
Among the last solo piano works Rachmaninoff completed.
Written in his leaner, more concentrated later style.

43.about: A set of twenty-four variations on the famous theme of Paganini’s 24th Caprice for solo violin, alternating brilliant virtuoso display with passages of deep lyricism, most famously the eighteenth variation, which inverts Paganini’s theme into a soaring, romantic melody that became one of Rachmaninoff’s most beloved tunes, later used in countless films.
43.ctx: Composed in 1934 at Rachmaninoff’s villa in Switzerland, one of the last major works he completed, drawing on the same Paganini theme that had already inspired variation sets by Brahms and Liszt, and incorporating, in several stormy variations, a quotation of the medieval Dies irae chant that recurs throughout much of Rachmaninoff’s output.
facts: Its famous 18th variation inverts Paganini’s theme into a soaring new melody.
One of the last major works Rachmaninoff completed.
Quotes the medieval Dies irae chant, a recurring motif throughout his music.

45.about: Rachmaninoff’s last completed work, a three-movement orchestral suite of enormous colour and nostalgia, incorporating a quotation of his own long-abandoned First Symphony in the first movement and, in the finale, the Dies irae chant set finally against a quotation of the Orthodox ’Blessed art Thou, O Lord’ from his All-Night Vigil — read by many as the composer’s own farewell.
45.ctx: Composed in 1940 at Rachmaninoff’s summer home on Long Island, the last major work he completed before his death three years later, drawing together threads — the Dies irae, Orthodox chant, echoes of his own earlier music — that had run through his entire creative life.
parts: A nostalgic opening movement quoting Rachmaninoff’s own First Symphony.
A finale combining the Dies irae with a quotation from his own All-Night Vigil.
facts: Rachmaninoff’s last completed work.
Quotes his own First Symphony and his choral work All-Night Vigil.
Widely interpreted as the composer’s musical farewell.

3/2.about: Nicknamed the ’Bells of Moscow’, this brief, weighty prelude became Rachmaninoff’s most famous single piece almost overnight, built on three massive, tolling chords that open the work and return to close it, framing an agitated, stormy central section. Rachmaninoff grew to resent the piece’s overwhelming popularity, which followed him for the rest of his life and which audiences constantly demanded as an encore.
3/2.ctx: Composed in 1892 when Rachmaninoff was only nineteen, part of a set of five character pieces, Op. 3, dedicated to his teacher Anton Arensky. Its sudden fame abroad, especially in America, meant Rachmaninoff, decades later, still could rarely give a recital without being asked to play it.
facts: Rachmaninoff’s first major success, composed at just nineteen.
He grew to resent how often audiences demanded it as an encore.
Known popularly as the ’Bells of Moscow’.

23/5.about: Marked ’Alla marcia’, one of Rachmaninoff’s most popular preludes, built on a bold, martial main theme framing a broad, lyrical central melody, combining the composer’s gift for sweeping Romantic melody with a driving rhythmic energy.
23/5.ctx: Composed in 1901, part of the ten preludes of Op. 23 written in the years following the triumphant success of the Second Piano Concerto, after Rachmaninoff had emerged from the severe depression and creative block that had followed the disastrous premiere of his First Symphony.
facts: One of the most frequently performed of Rachmaninoff’s twenty-four preludes.
Composed in the productive years following the success of his Second Piano Concerto.
Marked ’Alla marcia’ for its bold, march-like character.

32/12.about: A restless, melancholy prelude built on rippling, unbroken figuration under a wistful melody, often considered one of the most purely beautiful of Rachmaninoff’s twenty-four preludes, which together span every major and minor key in the tradition of Chopin’s Op. 28 and Bach’s Well-Tempered Clavier.
32/12.ctx: Composed in 1910 at Ivanovka, the Rachmaninoff family estate, as the last of the thirteen preludes of Op. 32, completing his cycle of twenty-four preludes across three opus numbers (Op. 3 No. 2, Op. 23, and Op. 32) that together cover all twenty-four keys.
facts: Completes Rachmaninoff’s cycle of twenty-four preludes across three opus numbers.
Composed at Ivanovka, the Rachmaninoff family’s country estate.
Regarded as one of the most lyrically beautiful of his preludes.

39/5.about: One of the most passionate and frequently performed of Rachmaninoff’s Étude-tableaux, marked ’Appassionato’, built on a driving, obsessive rhythmic figure and sweeping melodic lines of enormous emotional intensity.
39/5.ctx: Composed in 1916–17, among the last works Rachmaninoff completed in Russia before fleeing the country permanently following the 1917 Revolution, part of the second set of Étude-tableaux, Op. 39, whose titled ’picture studies’ Rachmaninoff deliberately left mysterious, refusing in most cases to explain what images inspired them.
facts: Composed shortly before Rachmaninoff permanently left Russia after the 1917 Revolution.
Marked ’Appassionato’ for its intense, driving character.
Rachmaninoff generally declined to explain the specific images behind his Étude-tableaux.

34/14.about: A wordless song for voice and piano, sung entirely on a vowel sound without text, built on one long, arching melodic line of extraordinary simplicity and emotional directness; it has become one of Rachmaninoff’s most beloved melodies, frequently arranged for cello, violin, orchestra and countless other combinations.
34/14.ctx: Composed in 1912 as the last of the Fourteen Songs, Op. 34, dedicated to the soprano Antonina Nezhdanova, who premiered it; the absence of any text has made the piece endlessly adaptable to instrumental arrangement, and it is now probably better known in its many instrumental versions than in its original vocal form.
34/14.sc: Voice and piano (or various instrumental arrangements)
facts: Sung entirely on a vowel sound, with no text.
Dedicated to the soprano Antonina Nezhdanova, who premiered it.
Now most often heard in one of its many instrumental arrangements.
